newsitem.title: UK: BOE sets banking supervision objectives.
newsitem.headline: BOE sets banking supervision objectives.

text.p: The Bank of England on Wednesday set out its objectives for the supervision of the banking industry, standards for supervisors and the processes it will use.
The statement follows the Bank's Review of Supervision published in July last year in the wake of the February 1995 collapse of British investment bank Barings.

The Bank sets out its principal objective, as charged under UK banking legislation, as that of supervising the industry and individual banks; to act in the interests of depositors; impose prudential standards; and fulfil its international role.
Other secondary roles are seen as protecting against illegal deposit taking; tackling financial crime; and monitoring the conduct of business although this is not the bank's direct responsibility.
The Bank's paper repeats the view that while the Banking Act aims to avoid bank failures, supervision can never guarantee that this will not happen.

"To attempt to avoid any bank failing would be unhealthy for the economy (as it would involve limits on competition, innovation and the taking of risk, and increase the costs of supervision); it would also be virtually impossible to achieve," the Bank's paper says.
The Bank also notes its responsibilities on systemic risk, even though these are not addressed in the Banking Act.
On standards for its supervisors, the Bank says its approach starts from the recognition that the managers of banks are responsible for their business.

It says it aims to make impartial judgements based on objective and careful analysis and that it is predisposed to market solutions and a belief in the benefits of fair competition and market discipline.
The Bank says it aims to have clear policies; to consult and persuade, rather than dictate; to be constructive; and to act firmly and quickly without discrimination.

It says its standards will be used to discharge its policy responsibilities, such as working to raise international standards and developing relations with other supervisors and assessing banks' business and risk profiles.
In a second paper, on which the Bank invited industry comments, it sets out its proposals for change on the way it satisfies itself on the adequacy of an institution's financial controls.

The Bank proposes that bank boards should make an annual written statement on their internal controls and that the Bank should meet separately with the reporting institution's auditing accountant in addition to the current trilateral meeting.
It also comes to the conclusion that current safeguards on the independence of auditors who are also an institution's external auditors are adequate.
